open_obligations: Check whether Hase et al. observed SGR above 100% in any setting.
Note that Sun et al.'s oracle is 'all levels', not 'hard only'.
Check whether the objection applies only with RL training.
out.other_title: Supervision Gap Recovered (SGR) metric for easy-to-hard generalization
out.rationale: Hase et al. define Supervision Gap Recovered with hard-data finetuning as the 100% reference. Sun et al. decline to define an SGR or PGR analogue because models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained on all levels, which would push such metrics above 100%; Sun et al. report generator performance on the MATH500 test set, with generators optionally optimised by the evaluator, while Hase et al. compare finetuning on easy, hard or no data (zero-shot).
out.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether a gap-recovered metric with a hard-data oracle as upper bound is suitable for easy-to-hard evaluation

text: The authors state they chose not to define terms analogous to the weak-to-strong performance gap recovered (Burns et al.) or the supervision gap recovered (Hase et al.), because models trained only on simpler tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained across all difficulty levels. They instead report absolute and relative generator performance on the MATH500 test set.
title: No PGR or SGR analogue because easy-only training can beat full training
